extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of language, scientific method, and anyone who must define technical terms
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for giving precise connotations to words used in science, philosophy, and common discourse — when to define, how to choose defining properties, and how to preserve historical and practical meaning. Emphasizes the relation between definitions and the propositions/principles they are meant to serve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions must serve a proposition or principle
rubrics_metrics.description: A definition has scientific value only when it is associated with some proposition or principle in which the term is employed; the question of definition becomes a question concerning truth when it expresses a tacitly assumed proposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always ask what principle or proposition the proposed definition is intended to express or make true. Do not attempt to define a term in isolation; tie the definition to its immediate use in stating a truth or hypothesis (example: 'uniform force' defined so as to continue to denote gravity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition is part of the business of discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: To define so that the definition has scientific value requires sagacity akin to that used in discovery; the act of defining presupposes a decided step in knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that proposing a definition often follows (or accompanies) having discerned what truth one is to state; definitions are not merely lexical exercises but intellectual moves in inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer properties that are obvious and central as defining marks
rubrics_metrics.description: If properties fit to be selected as marks of the class are obvious, familiar, and bear a great part in producing the general resemblance, the definition will be most felicitous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing defining characteristics, favor those that are commonly perceived and that explain the general similarity which led to the class; however, a less obvious property may be acceptable if it best marks the class (example: de Blainville's definition of life based on decomposition/recomposition).

rubrics_metrics.name: It may be right to define by non-obvious but best-marking properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes the best mark of a class is not a familiar property; such a property can be chosen provided it is truly the best indicator of membership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be willing to base definitions on discovered structural or causal properties rather than on surface features, when those deeper properties more reliably identify the class.

rubrics_metrics.name: When impracticable, accept multiple senses rather than force a single connotation
rubrics_metrics.description: There are frequent cases where no single connotation can be given to a word that preserves all its current uses and the truth of all propositions in which it occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not artificially force a one-size-fits-all definition when a term legitimately functions in several derived senses; acknowledge ambiguity and investigate transitions of meaning instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for transitive (derivative) applications of words
rubrics_metrics.description: Words often extend by gradual transference from one object to another (transitive applications), producing derivative meanings that may ultimately coalesce or remain distinct depending on the strength of associations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace the historical chain of associations when analyzing a term's meanings; distinguish casual/occasional associations from those that are natural, habitual, and thus likely to merge into a complex conception (examples: 'beautiful', 'loyalty').

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer restricting a term’s denotation rather than indiscriminate extension
rubrics_metrics.description: When rectifying a vague term that carries various associations, it is often better to give it a fixed connotation by restricting its use (excluding some common applications) than by extending it to include all agreeable or related things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid broadening a term so far that it ceases to connote the particular quality of interest (example: do not define 'beautiful' simply as 'agreeable'); restriction preserves distinctive meaning and prevents loss of subtle qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not discard historical connotation without deep knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: In attempting to fix a vague term, one must not discard portions of its connotation that the word previously carried unless advisedly and on the ground of deeper knowledge of the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve the elements of meaning that encode past experience and truth; anyone proposing to redefine a term should be acquainted with its history and the opinions it has served to express, because redefining can render formerly true propositions false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language conserves past experience—preserve that function when redefining
rubrics_metrics.description: Words act as depositaries of accumulated experience; altering their meanings risks losing inherited premises and the ability to transmit past insights to posterity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modifying terminology, ensure you are not unintentionally erasing the conceptual resources encoded in traditional usages; prefer changes that retain useful historical associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use predication to keep complex meanings alive
rubrics_metrics.description: Because words often suggest only part of their complex meaning in actual use, frequently predicating all the various properties of a name helps keep its fuller associations present in the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prevent degeneration of meaning, explicitly predicate the different properties linked to a term in propositions and teaching so that the full cluster of ideas remains connected to the word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of defining words at the point of least current meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons who observe that a word is used without meaning may fix its use according to the time's scantiest connotation, thereby broadening its denotation and potentially eliminating older meanings and truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid fixing a term based only on its most attenuated contemporary usage; investigate and respect fuller historical senses to prevent loss of valuable conceptual content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dictionaries give blunt expositions; history of a word is often a better guide
rubrics_metrics.description: Dictionary meanings mark a word broadly, but many collateral associations adhere to words over time that dictionaries omit; the history of a word can reveal the law by which its successive meanings were produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult the word’s historical usage and the habitual circumstances associated with it rather than relying solely on dictionary definitions when deciding on appropriate employment or on reforms of terminology (examples: 'gentleman', 'loyalty', 'pagan').

rubrics_metrics.name: Before finalizing a definition, know the class’s properties and their causal relations
rubrics_metrics.description: To judge how a class-name should be defined, one must know all properties common to the class and the relations of causation or dependence among those properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt a definitive terminological settling until you have investigated and understood the full range of properties and causal connections that characterize the class; a good definition often requires substantive empirical or theoretical knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions should facilitate use in expressing truth and further inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Unfolding conceptions by means of definitions is only serviceable to science when combined with immediate use of definitions in stating and testing truths (e.g., defining momentum after recognizing its empirical role).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure definitions are operationally useful — they should enable clear expression of hypotheses, facilitate measurement or comparison, and help in the process of discovery and testing.
